title: Acoustic comfort in educational buildings: An integrative review and new directions for future research
review_question: To understand the current acoustic conditions in education buildings, the effects of different acoustic conditions on occupants (including students and teachers), and identify research gaps to guide future studies.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Articles written in English, published within the past two decades (2003-2023), from Web of Science database. Excluded studies focused on non-academic areas (canteen, cafeteria, gyms), special students (autism, ADHD, hearing impairments), or fishing-related topics.

synthesis_conclusions: Three main research topics were identified: current acoustic conditions and improvements in educational buildings, impacts of acoustic quality on students' performance, and impacts of acoustic quality on occupants' health.
Most educational buildings exhibit substandard acoustic performance, with noise and reverberation levels exceeding recommended standards.

Poor acoustic quality negatively impacts students' academic performance (e.g., listening comprehension, reading comprehension) and health (e.g., headaches, fatigue, sleep disturbances, mental health).
Teachers' comfort and health are also negatively affected by poor classroom acoustics, leading to vocal symptoms, cognitive fatigue, and potential hearing loss.
Common data collection methods include measurement, questionnaire surveys, performance tests, and simulations, while data analysis often involves comparison, regression, and clustering.
Advanced techniques like EEG and machine learning are promising for future acoustic research in educational settings.
evidence_gaps: Limited research on effective noise control methods for educational buildings, especially regarding impact noise and sound insulation of facades/floors.
Need for more localized acoustic improvement solutions that consider individual differences in noise perception and sensitivity.
Further development and testing of individually controlled acoustic environment devices (ICNDs).
Wider application and testing of personal sound amplification systems (PASPs) in standard classrooms with average students.
More studies on the restorative effects of soundscapes in classrooms, particularly using physiological measurements and focusing on children.
Investigation of interactive effects between acoustic quality and other IEQ factors (thermal, visual, IAQ) in actual educational buildings, considering more than two factors simultaneously.
Application of electroencephalography (EEG) to understand direct impacts of acoustic conditions on students' brain activities, comfort, attention, and emotional states in educational settings.
Application of machine learning to predict occupants' acoustic comfort in classrooms.
Combining machine learning and EEG for more profound insights into acoustic studies in educational buildings.
heterogeneity_sources: Type, difficulty level, and duration of academic tests for external noise impacts.
Different noise perceptions among students for performance correlation with annoyance.
Individual characteristics of students for annoyance levels.
Assumptions and simplifications in acoustic simulations.
Bias and personal interpretation in questionnaire surveys.
Oversimplification in questionnaire design for children.

moderators.effect: Younger students are more susceptible to detrimental effects of noise and require more effort to listen to speech in noisy classrooms.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Negative impacts of babble noise are more evident for younger students due to developing language and cognition. Negative impacts of noise on performance are more pronounced for young children.

moderators.effect: Traffic noise consistently shows negative impacts, while aircraft/construction noise shows inconsistent impacts depending on test type, difficulty, and duration.

moderators.variable: Noise intensity, reverberation time (RT), individual student characteristics
moderators.effect: These factors influence the level of annoyance experienced by students.
Noise level impacts teachers' voice load and vocal symptoms more, while RT impacts teachers' perceptions of noise and social climate more.

limitations: The typical data collection methods (measurement, questionnaire survey, simulation, performance test) have inherent limitations in capturing the full complexity and variability of the relationships between acoustic quality and occupants.
Acoustic measurements are limited to specific locations and periods, costly, and time-consuming.
Questionnaire surveys are subject to bias, personal interpretation, and potential oversimplification.
Acoustic simulations are based on assumptions and simplifications, which may not fully reflect actual situations.
Performance tests are limited by time constraints and may not fully capture overall occupant performance, and other IEQ factors are not always rigorously controlled.
Most studies on restorative soundscapes focused on adults' perceptions and relied on self-reported surveys, which may be less accurate for young children.
ICND devices are in early stages and have identified shortcomings.
PASPs are not widely tested or applied in standard classrooms with average students.
EEG and machine learning applications in educational acoustics are still in exploratory phases.
